Add a `logger.info` inside `broadcast` to capture message volume. - **Metrics** – Expose a `/metrics` endpoint using `prometheus-client` (the book’s deployment chapter will cover exporting these metrics). --- ## Key Takeaways - FastAPI’s built‑in `WebSocket` support lets you add real‑time features without leaving the familiar FastAPI ecosystem. - A **central `ConnectionManager`** tracks sockets per room, enabling efficient broadcasting and private messaging. - **JWT authentication** can be applied during the WebSocket handshake, reusing the security utilities from the REST API chapter. - Room management is achieved by mapping room identifiers to sets of connections; the same pattern scales to private chats, topic channels, or group conversations. - For **high concurrency**, keep the code async, use multiple Uvicorn workers, and optionally employ Redis Pub/Sub for cross‑process broadcasting. - Deploy with Docker (as shown in earlier chapters), configure environment variables for secrets, and use a CI/CD pipeline to automate releases. By the end of this chapter you have a fully functional, secure, and deployable real‑time chat application that can serve as a standout piece in your Python portfolio.

modules.title: Creating a Document Processing System with Python
modules.content: ## Why Document Processing Matters Imagine a small law firm that receives dozens of contracts, court filings, and scanned letters every week. Every new document must be searchable, its key clauses indexed, and any deadlines flagged—otherwise the firm risks missing critical dates. Manually opening each PDF, copying text into a spreadsheet, and hunting for a due‑date is a recipe for error and lost billable hours. A **document processing system** built with Python can automate the entire workflow: * Pull raw text from PDFs and Word files. * Run OCR on scanned images to unlock hidden text. * Extract dates, contract numbers, and parties using regex/NLP. * Store the results in a searchable database behind a FastAPI endpoint. The following sections walk you through a production‑ready implementation that you can add to your portfolio and extend for any domain that works with documents. --- ## Project Architecture Overview Leverage the **production‑grade structure** introduced when we built the FastAPI API earlier: ``` docproc/ ├─ src/ │ ├─ docproc/ │ │ ├─ __init__.py │ │ ├─ core/ │ │ │ ├─ pdf.py │ │ │ ├─ word.py │ │ │ ├─ ocr.py │ │ │ └─ extractor.py │ │ ├─ db/ │ │ │ └─ models.py │ │ └─ api/ │ │ └─ routes.py ├─ tests/ │ └─ … ├─ pyproject.toml └─ README.md ``` * **Poetry** continues to manage dependencies and virtual environments. * **FastAPI** provides the HTTP layer for uploading documents and searching results. * **SQLite with FTS5** (or Elasticsearch for larger deployments) offers full‑text search. All code lives under `src/docproc/`, keeping the public API clean and the internal modules isolated—a pattern you already adopted in the earlier FastAPI chapter. --- ## Setting Up Dependencies ```bash # Activate Poetry for the project (assumes Poetry already installed) poetry new docproc cd docproc poetry add fastapi uvicorn[standard] python-multipart poetry add pypdf2 pdfplumber python-docx pillow pytesseract poetry add spacy poetry add "sqlite-utils[fts5]" # optional, for easier FTS5 handling poetry run python -m spacy download en_core_web_sm ``` **Tesseract OCR** is an external binary, not a Python package. Install it per OS: | OS | Command | |----|---------| | macOS | `brew install tesseract` | | Ubuntu/Debian | `sudo apt-get install tesseract-ocr` | | Windows | Download the installer from the [official repo](https://github.com/tesseract-ocr/tesseract) and add its `bin` directory to `PATH`. | Add a pre‑commit hook to enforce **Black**, **flake8**, and **isort** (already set up in the repo template) so the new modules stay clean. --- ## PDF Extraction Strategies ### Choosing the Right Tool | Library | Strength | When to Prefer | |---------|----------|----------------| | **PyPDF2** | Fast, works on most PDFs, simple API | Text‑only PDFs, no need for layout details | | **pdfplumber** | Retains layout, can extract tables and exact coordinates | PDFs with complex columns, tables, or mixed text/image content | Both libraries are pure Python, so they play nicely with Poetry. ### Example: Extracting Text from a Multi‑Page PDF ```python # src/docproc/core/pdf.py import io from typing import List import PyPDF2 import pdfplumber def extract_text_pypdf2(path: str) -> str: """Quick extraction when layout is not critical.""" with open(path, "rb") as f: reader = PyPDF2.PdfReader(f) return "\n".join(page.extract_text() or "" for page in reader.pages) def extract_text_pdfplumber(path: str) -> str: """Preserves column order and can pull tables.""" texts: List[str] = [] with pdfplumber.open(path) as pdf: for page in pdf.pages: texts.append(page.extract_text()) return "\n".join(filter(None, texts)) ``` **Usage** ```python >>> from docproc.core.pdf import extract_text_pdfplumber >>> txt = extract_text_pdfplumber("samples/contract.pdf") >>> print(txt[:200]) # preview first 200 characters ``` The function returns a clean string ready for downstream regex/NLP processing. --- ## Word Document Handling with `python-docx` ### Reading, Modifying, and Saving ```python # src/docproc/core/word.py from pathlib import Path import docx def read_docx(path: Path) -> str: """Concatenate all paragraph texts in a .docx file.""" document = docx.Document(path) return "\n".join(p.text for p in document.paragraphs) def extract_headings(path: Path) -> dict: """Return a mapping of heading level → text.""" document = docx.Document(path) headings = {} for para in document.paragraphs: if para.style.name.startswith("Heading"): level = int(para.style.name.split()[-1]) # e.g., Heading 2 → 2 headings.setdefault(level, []).append(para.text) return headings ``` ### Example: Pulling Out Tables from an Invoice ```python def extract_tables(path: Path) -> list[list[list[str]]]: """Return a list of tables; each table is a list of rows, each row a list of cell texts.""" doc = docx.Document(path) tables_data = [] for table in doc.tables: rows = [] for row in table.rows: rows.append([cell.text for cell in row.cells]) tables_data.append(rows) return tables_data ``` You can now feed the raw text or the tabular data into the same extraction pipeline used for PDFs. --- ## OCR for Scanned Documents ### Installing Tesseract Make sure the `tesseract` command is reachable from the shell (`tesseract -v` should print the version). ### Using `pytesseract` ```python # src/docproc/core/ocr.py from pathlib import Path from PIL import Image import pytesseract def ocr_image(image_path: Path, lang: str = "eng") -> str: """Run OCR on a single image file.""" img = Image.open(image_path) return pytesseract.image_to_string(img, lang=lang) def ocr_pdf(pdf_path: Path, lang: str = "eng") -> str: """Convert each PDF page to an image then OCR.""" import pdf2image # optional dependency for PDF → image conversion pages = pdf2image.convert_from_path(str(pdf_path)) texts = [pytesseract.image_to_string(page, lang=lang) for page in pages] return "\n".join(texts) ``` > **Tip:** Tesseract performs best on 300 dpi images. If you encounter low‑quality scans, consider preprocessing with Pillow (e.g., `Image.filter`, `Image.convert('L')`). ### Example: Processing a Scanned Invoice ```python >>> from docproc.core.ocr import ocr_image >>> txt = ocr_image(Path("samples/scanned_invoice.jpg")) >>> "Total Due:" in txt True ``` Now the OCR output can be piped into the same regex/NLP extractor used for native PDFs. --- ## Structured Data Extraction ### Regular Expressions for Dates, IDs, and Money ```python import re from typing import Tuple, List, Optional DATE_RE = re.compile(r"\b(?:\d{1,2}[/-]){2}\d{2,4}\b") MONEY_RE = re.compile(r"\b[$€£]\s?\d{1,3}(?:,\d{3})*(?:\.\d{2})?\b") INVOICE_RE = re.compile(r"\bInvoice\s*#?\s*[:\-]?\s*(\w+)\b", re.I) def find_dates(text: str) -> List[str]: return DATE_RE.findall(text) def find_money(text: str) -> List[str]: return MONEY_RE.findall(text) def find_invoice_number(text: str) -> Optional[str]: m = INVOICE_RE.search(text) return m.group(1) if m else None ``` ### Light NLP with spaCy for Entity Extraction ```python import spacy nlp = spacy.load("en_core_web_sm") def extract_entities(text: str) -> List[Tuple[str, str]]: """Return a list of (entity_text, label) tuples.""" doc = nlp(text) return [(ent.text, ent.label_) for ent in doc.ents] ``` ### Example: Pulling Contract Parties from Mixed Text ```python >>> sample = """ ... This Agreement is made between Acme Corp ("Seller") and ... Beta Industries ("Buyer") on 12/05/2023. ... """ >>> extract_entities(sample) [('Acme Corp', 'ORG'), ('Beta Industries', 'ORG'), ('12/05/2023', 'DATE')] ``` Combine regex (for precise patterns) with spaCy (for context‑aware entities) to build a robust data model. --- ## Building a Searchable Index ### Choosing Storage * **SQLite + FTS5** – lightweight, zero‑config, perfect for a portfolio demo. * **Elasticsearch** – scalable, distributed, ideal for production‑grade corpora. Below we illustrate the SQLite approach; swapping to Elasticsearch only requires changing the `insert` and `search` functions. ### Defining the Schema ```python # src/docproc/db/models.py import sqlite3 from pathlib import Path DB_PATH = Path(__file__).with_name("documents.db") def init_db(): conn = sqlite3.connect(DB_PATH) conn.execute( """ CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE IF NOT EXISTS docs USING fts5( file_name, content, invoice_number, parties, dates, money, tokenize = "porter" ); """ ) conn.commit() conn.close() ``` ### Inserting Processed Records ```python def add_document( file_name: str, content: str, invoice_number: str | None = None, parties: str | None = None, dates: str | None = None, money: str | None = None, ): conn = sqlite3.connect(DB_PATH) conn.execute( """ INSERT INTO docs (file_name, content, invoice_number, parties, dates, money) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?); """, (file_name, content, invoice_number, parties, dates, money), ) conn.commit() conn.close() ``` ### Query API via FastAPI ```python # src/docproc/api/routes.py from fastapi import APIRouter, UploadFile, File from docproc.core import pdf, word, ocr, extractor from docproc.db.models import add_document, init_db router = APIRouter() init_db() # ensure tables exist on startup @router.post("/upload") async def upload(file: UploadFile = File(...)): suffix = Path(file.filename).suffix.lower() raw_bytes = await file.read() temp_path = Path("/tmp") / file.filename temp_path.write_bytes(raw_bytes) # 1️⃣ Extract raw text if suffix == ".pdf": text = pdf.extract_text_pdfplumber(str(temp_path)) elif suffix in {".docx", ".doc"}: text = word.read_docx(temp_path) else: # assume image for OCR text = ocr.ocr_image(temp_path) # 2️⃣ Structured extraction invoice = extractor.find_invoice_number(text) dates = ", ".join(extractor.find_dates(text)) money = ", ".join(extractor.find_money(text)) parties = ", ".join([e[0] for e in extractor.extract_entities(text) if e[1] == "ORG"]) # 3️⃣ Store in DB add_document( file_name=file.filename, content=text, invoice_number=invoice, parties=parties, dates=dates, money=money, ) return {"status": "ok", "invoice": invoice} @router.get("/search") def search(q: str): conn = sqlite3.connect(DB_PATH) cur = conn.execute("SELECT file_name, snippet(docs, -1, '', '', '...', 10) AS snippet FROM docs WHERE docs MATCH ?", (q,)) results = [{"file": row[0], "snippet": row[1]} for row in cur.fetchall()] conn.close() return results ``` Add the router to the FastAPI app (see the earlier FastAPI chapter) and run: ```bash poetry run uvicorn docproc.api.main:app --reload ``` You now have a **single endpoint** for uploading any supported document and another for full‑text search across the processed corpus. --- ## Putting It All Together: A Minimal Document Processor Service ### Directory Layout Recap ``` docproc/ ├─ src/ │ ├─ docproc/ │ │ ├─ core/ │ │ │ ├─ __init__.py │ │ │ ├─ pdf.py │ │ │ ├─ word.py │ │ │ ├─ ocr.py │ │ │ └─ extractor.py # regex + spaCy helpers │ │ ├─ db/ │ │ │ └─ models.py │ │ └─ api/ │ │ ├─ __init__.py │ │ └─ routes.py │ └─ main.py # FastAPI app entry point ├─ tests/ │ └─ … ├─ pyproject.toml └─ README.md ``` ### Core Processing Pipeline (simplified) ```python # src/docproc/core/extractor.py from .pdf import extract_text_pdfplumber from .word import read_docx from .ocr import ocr_image from .pdf import extract_text_pypdf2 import re import spacy nlp = spacy.load("en_core_web_sm") DATE_RE = re.compile(r"\b(?:\d{1,2}[/-]){2}\d{2,4}\b") MONEY_RE = re.compile(r"\b[$€£]\s?\d{1,3}(?:,\d{3})*(?:\.\d{2})?\b") INVOICE_RE = re.compile(r"\bInvoice\s*#?\s*[:\-]?\s*(\w+)\b", re.I) def process_file(path: Path) -> dict: suffix = path.suffix.lower() if suffix == ".pdf": raw = extract_text_pdfplumber(str(path)) elif suffix in {".docx", ".doc"}: raw = read_docx(path) else: # image raw = ocr_image(path) # Structured data invoice = INVOICE_RE.search(raw) dates = DATE_RE.findall(raw) money = MONEY_RE.findall(raw) entities = [(ent.text, ent.label_) for ent in nlp(raw).ents] parties = [t for t, l in entities if l == "ORG"] return { "content": raw, "invoice_number": invoice.group(1) if invoice else None, "dates": dates, "money": money, "parties": parties, } ``` ### FastAPI Entry Point ```python # src/main.py from fastapi import FastAPI from docproc.api.routes import router app = FastAPI(title="Document Processor") app.include_router(router, prefix="/api") ``` Run with the same `uvicorn` command as before. The service is now ready for integration with a front‑end, CI pipeline, or container deployment (the next chapter will cover cloud deployment). --- ## Testing & Quality Assurance * **Unit tests** – write a test for each core module (`tests/test_pdf.py`, `tests/test_ocr.py`). Use the `pytest` fixture `tmp_path` to create temporary files. * **Pre‑commit** – the repo already ships with Black, flake8, and isort checks; add `pytest --maxfail=1 --disable-warnings` to the hook list to enforce test passing before each commit. * **Type hints** – the codebase already uses static typing; run `mypy src` to keep the type surface clean. These practices echo the disciplined workflow you adopted when building the RESTful API earlier. --- ## Performance Considerations * **Batch processing** – for large uploads, queue files with **Celery** (covered in an earlier chapter) and let workers call `process_file`. * **Async I/O** – FastAPI can stream uploads without loading the whole file into memory (`UploadFile` already uses `SpooledTemporaryFile`). * **Caching** – store OCR results in a separate table keyed by file hash to avoid re‑processing identical scans. These optimizations become important when scaling beyond a demo dataset. --- ## Key Takeaways * **PDFs, Word docs, and scanned images** can all be turned into plain text with `PyPDF2`, `pdfplumber`, `python-docx`, and `pytesseract`. * **Regular expressions** excel at precise pattern matching (dates, money, invoice numbers), while **spaCy** adds contextual entity extraction. * A **full‑text searchable index**—SQLite + FTS5 for a quick demo or Elasticsearch for production—lets you retrieve documents by keyword, entity, or extracted field. * By reusing the **FastAPI + Poetry** architecture from earlier chapters, you can expose upload and search endpoints with minimal boilerplate. * Adding tests, type hints, and pre‑commit hooks preserves code quality, and optional Celery integration prepares the system for high‑throughput workloads. With these building blocks, you now have a functional, extensible document processing pipeline ready to showcase in your portfolio or to expand for real‑world projects.

modules.title: Developing a Multi-threaded Web Crawler
modules.content:
## Why Crawl When You Can Conquer

Imagine you need to monitor the latest articles on dozens of tech blogs, extract their headlines, and feed them into a recommendation engine that updates every hour. Manually visiting each site is impossible; a well‑behaved, high‑performance crawler can do the heavy lifting while staying polite to the servers it visits. This chapter walks you through building exactly that: a multi‑threaded web crawler that respects *robots.txt*, throttles itself appropriately, avoids duplicate work, and persists the harvested data in a database ready for downstream analytics.

---

## Project Scaffold – Leveraging What You Already Built

If you followed the earlier chapters on **FastAPI**, **Poetry**, and the **production‑grade project layout**, you already have a solid foundation:

- **Poetry** for dependency management (`poetry init` → `poetry add requests beautifulsoup4 sqlalchemy aiosqlite`)
- A **src/** package with clear separation (`crawler/`, `models/`, `utils/`)
- **Pre‑commit** hooks (`black`, `flake8`, `isort`) ensuring clean code

Create a new module under `src/crawler/` called `engine.py`. This will house the core crawling logic, while `src/models/` will contain the SQLAlchemy ORM definitions. Keeping the structure consistent with previous chapters makes the codebase instantly familiar and ready for future expansion (e.g., exposing a FastAPI endpoint that triggers a crawl).

```bash
poetry new multi_threaded_crawler
cd multi_threaded_crawler
poetry add requests beautifulsoup4 sqlalchemy aiosqlite
mkdir -p src/crawler src/models src/utils
```

---

## 1. The Bare‑Bones Crawler

Before we add concurrency, let’s implement a simple, single‑threaded crawler that fetches a page and extracts links.

```python
# src/crawler/basic.py
import time
from urllib.parse import urljoin, urlparse

import requests
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup


def fetch(url: str, timeout: int = 10) -> str:
    """Return the raw HTML of *url* or raise an exception."""
    response = requests.get(url, timeout=timeout, headers={"User-Agent": "MyCrawler/1.0"})
    response.raise_for_status()
    return response.text


def extract_links(html: str, base_url: str) -> set[str]:
    """Return absolute URLs found in *html*."""
    soup = BeautifulSoup(html, "html.parser")
    links = {
        urljoin(base_url, tag.get("href"))
        for tag in soup.find_all("a", href=True)
        if tag.get("href").strip()
    }
    # Filter out fragments and mailto links
    return {link.split("#")[0] for link in links if not link.startswith("mailto:")}


def crawl(start_url: str, max_pages: int = 100) -> None:
    visited = set()
    frontier = [start_url]

    while frontier and len(visited) < max_pages:
        url = frontier.pop(0)
        if url in visited:
            continue
        try:
            html = fetch(url)
        except Exception as exc:
            print(f"[!] Failed {url}: {exc}")
            continue

        visited.add(url)
        print(f"[+] Visited {url}")

        for link in extract_links(html, url):
            if urlparse(link).netloc == urlparse(start_url).netloc:
                frontier.append(link)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    crawl("https://realpython.com/")
```

**What this snippet demonstrates**

- **Requests** for HTTP handling.
- **BeautifulSoup** for parsing HTML.
- A *frontier* list that drives breadth‑first traversal.
- Simple duplicate avoidance via the `visited` set.

Run it to see the crawler traverse a single domain. The next sections will make it *polite*, *fast*, and *persistent*.

---

## 2. Playing Nice – robots.txt and Crawl Delays

Webmasters publish a `robots.txt` file to declare which parts of a site are off‑limits to crawlers. Ignoring it can get your IP banned or, worse, land you in legal trouble. Python ships with `urllib.robotparser`, a lightweight parser that we can wrap in a utility class.

```python
# src/utils/robots.py
from urllib import robotparser
from urllib.parse import urlparse
import time
import threading


class RobotsGuard:
    """Cache‑aware robots.txt checker with per‑host crawl‑delay."""

    _parsers: dict[str, robotparser.RobotFileParser] = {}
    _delays: dict[str, float] = {}
    _lock = threading.Lock()

    def __init__(self, user_agent: str = "MyCrawler/1.0"):
        self.user_agent = user_agent

    def _get_parser(self, netloc: str) -> robotparser.RobotFileParser:
        with self._lock:
            if netloc not in self._parsers:
                rp = robotparser.RobotFileParser()
                rp.set_url(f"https://{netloc}/robots.txt")
                rp.read()
                self._parsers[netloc] = rp
            return self._parsers[netloc]

    def can_fetch(self, url: str) -> bool:
        parsed = urlparse(url)
        rp = self._get_parser(parsed.netloc)
        return rp.can_fetch(self.user_agent, url)

    def get_delay(self, url: str) -> float:
        parsed = urlparse(url)
        netloc = parsed.netloc
        if netloc not in self._delays:
            rp = self._get_parser(netloc)
            delay = rp.crawl_delay(self.user_agent) or 1.0  # default 1 s
            self._delays[netloc] = delay
        return self._delays[netloc]

    def respect_delay(self, url: str):
        """Sleep the required amount before issuing the next request."""
        delay = self.get_delay(url)
        time.sleep(delay)
```

**Key points**

- **Caching**: We keep a parser per host to avoid repeated network calls.
- **Thread safety**: A simple `Lock` protects the shared dictionaries.
- **Default delay**: If the site omits `Crawl‑delay`, we fall back to a courteous 1 second pause.

Integrate the guard into the crawler:

```python
# src/crawler/basic.py (updated)
from src.utils.robots import RobotsGuard

guard = RobotsGuard()

def crawl(start_url: str, max_pages: int = 100) -> None:
    # ... unchanged initialization
    while frontier and len(visited) < max_pages:
        url = frontier.pop(0)
        if url in visited or not guard.can_fetch(url):
            continue

        guard.respect_delay(url)          # <-- politeness enforced here
        # ... fetch, parse, enqueue as before
```

Now the crawler automatically backs off according to each site’s policy, dramatically reducing the risk of being blocked.

---

## 3. Detecting Duplicates – Normalization & Bloom Filters

A naive `set` works for small crawls, but as the frontier grows into the hundreds of thousands of URLs, memory consumption spikes. Two techniques keep duplicate detection lightweight:

1. **URL Normalization** – strip query parameters that don’t affect content (e.g., `?ref=twitter`), sort remaining parameters, and lowercase the scheme/host.
2. **Bloom Filter** – a probabilistic data structure that uses a fixed amount of memory and offers *fast* membership checks with a tolerable false‑positive rate.

### 3.1 Normalization Helper

```python
# src/utils/url.py
from urllib.parse import urlparse, urlunparse, parse_qsl, urlencode


def normalize(url: str) -> str:
    """Return a canonical representation of *url*."""
    parsed = urlparse(url)
    # Lowercase scheme and netloc
    scheme = parsed.scheme.lower()
    netloc = parsed.netloc.lower()
    # Sort query parameters, drop tracking keys
    query = sorted(
        (k, v) for k, v in parse_qsl(parsed.query, keep_blank_values=True)
        if k not in {"utm_source", "utm_medium", "utm_campaign"}
    )
    query_str = urlencode(query, doseq=True)
    # Rebuild URL without fragment
    return urlunparse((scheme, netloc, parsed.path.rstrip("/"), "", query_str, ""))
```

### 3.2 Bloom Filter Wrapper

```python
# src/utils/bloom.py
import math
import hashlib
import threading


class BloomFilter:
    """Thread‑safe Bloom filter with a configurable false‑positive rate."""

    def __init__(self, expected_items: int = 1_000_000, fp_rate: float = 0.001):
        self.size = -int(expected_items * math.log(fp_rate) / (math.log(2) ** 2))
        self.hash_count = int((self.size / expected_items) * math.log(2))
        self.bit_array = bytearray(self.size // 8 + 1)
        self.lock = threading.Lock()

    def _hashes(self, item: str):
        digest = hashlib.sha256(item.encode()).digest()
        for i in range(self.hash_count):
            yield int.from_bytes(digest[i * 2 : i * 2 + 2], "big") % self.size

    def add(self, item: str):
        with self.lock:
            for pos in self._hashes(item):
                self.bit_array[pos // 8] |= 1 << (pos % 8)

    def __contains__(self, item: str) -> bool:
        with self.lock:
            return all(
                self.bit_array[pos // 8] & (1 << (pos % 8))
                for pos in self._hashes(item)
            )
```

**Usage in the crawler**

```python
# src/crawler/basic.py (updated)
from src.utils.url import normalize
from src.utils.bloom import BloomFilter

visited = BloomFilter()
frontier = [start_url]

while frontier and len(visited) < max_pages:
    raw_url = frontier.pop(0)
    url = normalize(raw_url)
    if url in visited or not guard.can_fetch(url):
        continue

    guard.respect_delay(url)
    # fetch, parse, etc.
    visited.add(url)
```

The Bloom filter dramatically reduces memory pressure while still guaranteeing that we never *re‑visit* a URL we have already processed (modulo the tiny false‑positive probability).

---

## 4. Concurrency Choices – Threading vs asyncio

Python offers two primary models for concurrent I/O:

| Feature | **Threading** (via `concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor`) | **asyncio** (`aiohttp`, `asyncio.gather`) |
|---------|------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------|
| **Implementation** | Familiar, blocking APIs (requests, BeautifulSoup) | Requires async‑compatible libraries |
| **CPU‑bound work** | GIL limits parallelism; still fine for I/O‑heavy tasks | Same limitation, but event loop is lightweight |
| **Learning curve** | Low – just wrap functions in a pool | Higher – need to rewrite code to be async |
| **Performance** | Good for dozens of concurrent connections; limited by thread overhead | Excellent for hundreds–thousands of connections |
| **Error handling** | Exceptions propagate as `Future` results | Exceptions need `await` handling |

Because this chapter targets **intermediate learners** who already know `requests` and `BeautifulSoup`, we’ll start with a **thread‑based** implementation. Later, a short `asyncio` alternative will be sketched so readers can experiment.

---

## 5. Multi‑Threaded Crawler Implementation

### 5.1 Shared Data Structures

- **Frontier Queue** – a thread‑safe `queue.Queue`.
- **Visited Bloom Filter** – already thread‑safe.
- **Result Store** – a SQLAlchemy session scoped per thread.

```python
# src/crawler/threaded.py
import queue
import threading
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor, as_completed

import requests
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup

from src.utils.robots import RobotsGuard
from src.utils.url import normalize
from src.utils.bloom import BloomFilter
from src.models.page import Page, get_session

NUM_WORKERS = 8
MAX_PAGES = 5_000

frontier = queue.Queue()
visited = BloomFilter()
guard = RobotsGuard()
```

### 5.2 Worker Function

```python
def worker(thread_id: int):
    session = get_session()               # scoped session per thread
    while True:
        try:
            raw_url = frontier.get_nowait()
        except queue.Empty:
            break

        url = normalize(raw_url)
        if url in visited or not guard.can_fetch(url):
            frontier.task_done()
            continue

        guard.respect_delay(url)
        try:
            resp = requests.get(url, timeout=10,
                                headers={"User-Agent": guard.user_agent})
            resp.raise_for_status()
        except Exception as exc:
            print(f"[T{thread_id}] error {url}: {exc}")
            frontier.task_done()
            continue

        visited.add(url)
        soup = BeautifulSoup(resp.text, "html.parser")
        title = soup.title.string.strip() if soup.title else "Untitled"

        # Persist the page record
        page = Page(url=url, title=title, fetched_at=datetime.utcnow())
        session.add(page)
        session.commit()

        # Enqueue new links (same domain only)
        base = urlparse(url).netloc
        for link in extract_links(resp.text, url):
            if urlparse(link).netloc == base:
                frontier.put_nowait(link)

        frontier.task_done()
        print(f"[T{thread_id}] crawled {url}")
```

### 5.3 Orchestrator

```python
def start_crawl(seed: str):
    frontier.put_nowait(seed)

    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=NUM_WORKERS) as executor:
        futures = [executor.submit(worker, i) for i in range(NUM_WORKERS)]
        # Wait for all workers to finish
        for future in as_completed(futures):
            future.result()   # re‑raise any exception

if __name__ == "__main__":
    start_crawl("https://news.ycombinator.com/")
```

**What we gain**

- **Parallel I/O** – up to `NUM_WORKERS` simultaneous connections.
- **Graceful shutdown** – `queue.task_done()` and `queue.join()` (omitted for brevity) ensure all pending URLs are processed before the program exits.
- **Database persistence** – each thread commits its own `Page` objects, avoiding cross‑thread session conflicts.

---

## 6. AsyncIO Alternative (Optional)

If you prefer to push the concurrency ceiling, replace the blocking `requests` with `aiohttp` and the synchronous `BeautifulSoup` with `selectolax` (or keep BeautifulSoup via `run_in_executor`). Below is a minimal sketch:

```python
# src/crawler/async_crawler.py
import asyncio
from aiohttp import ClientSession, TCPConnector
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup

from src.utils.robots import RobotsGuard
from src.utils.url import normalize
from src.utils.bloom import BloomFilter

guard = RobotsGuard()
visited = BloomFilter()
MAX_CONCURRENCY = 100
semaphore = asyncio.Semaphore(MAX_CONCURRENCY)


async def fetch(session: ClientSession, url: str) -> str:
    async with semaphore:
        async with session.get(url, headers={"User-Agent": guard.user_agent}) as resp:
            resp.raise_for_status()
            return await resp.text()


async def crawl(start_url: str):
    async with ClientSession(connector=TCPConnector(limit_per_host=MAX_CONCURRENCY)) as session:
        to_visit = asyncio.Queue()
        await to_visit.put(start_url)

        while not to_visit.empty():
            raw = await to_visit.get()
            url = normalize(raw)
            if url in visited or not guard.can_fetch(url):
                to_visit.task_done()
                continue

            html = await fetch(session, url)
            visited.add(url)

            soup = BeautifulSoup(html, "html.parser")
            # ... store in DB (use async SQLAlchemy if desired) ...

            for link in extract_links(html, url):
                await to_visit.put(link)

            to_visit.task_done()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(crawl("https://realpython.com/"))
```

The async version can sustain **hundreds** of concurrent connections with a modest memory footprint, but it demands a shift to async‑compatible libraries for every I/O operation.

---

## 7. Persisting Crawl Data – SQLAlchemy + SQLite (or PostgreSQL)

For a portfolio project, **SQLite** is sufficient and eliminates external dependencies. Yet, the ORM model we define can be swapped for PostgreSQL with a single connection‑string change—showcasing the portability emphasized in the earlier **FastAPI** chapter.

```python
# src/models/page.py
from datetime import datetime

from sqlalchemy import Column, String, DateTime, Integer, create_engine
from sqlalchemy.orm import declarative_base, sessionmaker

Base = declarative_base()
engine = create_engine("sqlite:///crawler.db", echo=False, future=True)
SessionLocal = sessionmaker(bind=engine, expire_on_commit=False)


class Page(Base):
    __tablename__ = "pages"

    id = Column(Integer, primary_key=True, index=True)
    url = Column(String, unique=True, nullable=False, index=True)
    title = Column(String, nullable=False)
    fetched_at = Column(DateTime, default=datetime.utcnow)


def init_db():
    Base.metadata.create_all(bind=engine)


def get_session():
    return SessionLocal()
```

Run `init_db()` once (e.g., from a small script) to create the schema. The `Page` model captures the minimal metadata needed for most downstream analytics: the URL, its title, and a timestamp.

### Real‑World Example: Building a News Headline Archive

```python
# src/crawler/examples/news_archive.py
from src.crawler.threaded import start_crawl
from src.models.page import init_db, Page, get_session

def archive_hn():
    init_db()
    start_crawl("https://news.ycombinator.com/")
    # After the crawl, query the DB for the latest headlines
    session = get_session()
    recent = session.query(Page).order_by(Page.fetched_at.desc()).limit(20).all()
    for p in recent:
        print(f"{p.fetched_at:%Y-%m-%d %H:%M} – {p.title}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    archive_hn()
```

Running the script populates `crawler.db` with thousands of Hacker News article URLs and titles, then prints the most recent 20 entries. This concrete artifact can be showcased on GitHub, linked to a simple FastAPI endpoint that returns the stored headlines as JSON.

---

## 8. Robustness – Retries, Timeouts, and Logging

A production‑grade crawler must survive flaky networks and malformed pages.

### 8.1 Exponential Back‑off Retries

```python
import backoff  # pip install backoff

@backoff.on_exception(backoff.expo, requests.RequestException, max_tries=5)
def fetch_with_retry(url: str) -> str:
    resp = requests.get(url, timeout=10, headers={"User-Agent": guard.user_agent})
    resp.raise_for_status()
    return resp.text
```

Replace the direct `requests.get` call with `fetch_with_retry`. The decorator automatically retries with increasing delays, capping after five attempts.

### 8.2 Structured Logging

```python
import logging

log = logging.getLogger("crawler")
log.setLevel(logging.INFO)
handler = logging.StreamHandler()
formatter = logging.Formatter("%(asctime)s %(levelname)s [%(threadName)s] %(message)s")
handler.setFormatter(formatter)
log.addHandler(handler)
```

Swap `print` statements for `log.info`, `log.warning`, and `log.error`. The consistent format aids later debugging and integrates nicely with the logging configuration you may have set up for your FastAPI services.

---

## 9. Performance Tweaks – Connection Pooling & Thread Count

- **Reuse a `requests.Session`** per worker to benefit from HTTP keep‑alive.  
  ```python
  session = requests.Session()
  response = session.get(url, timeout=10)
  ```
- **Tune `NUM_WORKERS`** based on the target site’s `Crawl‑delay`. A high delay often means you can increase workers without overwhelming the server.
- **Batch DB writes**: accumulate `Page` objects and `session.bulk_save_objects` every 100 records to reduce transaction overhead.

---

## 10. Real‑World Scenarios

### 10.1 Price‑Tracker for E‑Commerce

A retailer wants daily snapshots of product prices across competitor sites. Using the crawler:

1. Seed URLs are the product listing pages.
2. The extraction logic focuses on price elements (`<span class="price">`).
3. Results are stored in a `prices` table with columns `product_id`, `competitor`, `price`, `scraped_at`.
4. A scheduled FastAPI endpoint triggers the crawl nightly, feeding data into a dashboard built with Plotly Dash (see Chapter 6).

### 10.2 Academic Paper Indexer

A research group needs a searchable index of recent papers from open‑access journals. The crawler:

- Starts from each journal’s RSS feed URL.
- Parses the article page for title, authors, abstract, and PDF link.
- Persists the metadata in a PostgreSQL database.
- Exposes a FastAPI search endpoint that returns JSON results for downstream ML pipelines (Chapter 8).

### 10.3 Sitemap Generator

A small website owner wants a dynamically generated `sitemap.xml`. The crawler:

- Traverses the entire public domain.
- Records each URL and its last‑modified date.
- Writes an XML file compliant with the sitemap protocol.
- The generated file can be served by a FastAPI route for SEO purposes.

Each example showcases a different downstream use case while reusing the same core crawler components.

---

## 11. Testing the Crawler

Unit‑testing a network‑heavy component can be tricky. Use **responses** (for `requests`) and **aioresponses** (for `aiohttp`) to mock HTTP calls, and **pytest‑asyncio** for async tests. Example for the basic fetch function:

```python
import responses
from src.crawler.basic import fetch

@responses.activate
def test_fetch_success():
    responses.add(responses.GET, "https://example.com",
                  body="<html></html>", status=200)
    html = fetch("https://example.com")
    assert "<html>" in html
```

Running the test suite under the same **pre‑commit** hooks ensures code quality stays high as you evolve the crawler.

---

## 12. Deploying the Crawler

Although deployment is covered later (Chapter 14), a quick note: packaging the crawler as a **Docker container** with the same `Poetry` lock file guarantees reproducible builds. The container can be orchestrated by **Celery** (Chapter 7) for scheduled runs, or by a simple cron job on a VM. The modular design—separating crawling, persistence, and API layers—makes such integration painless.

---

## Key Takeaways

- **Politeness first**: Honor `robots.txt` and apply per‑host crawl delays with a reusable `RobotsGuard`.
- **Duplicate avoidance**: Combine URL normalization with a Bloom filter to keep memory usage low while preventing re‑crawls.
- **Concurrency models**: Thread‑based crawling is accessible and fast enough for moderate workloads; `asyncio` scales to thousands of connections at the cost of a steeper learning curve.
- **Persistence matters**: Store extracted data with SQLAlchemy; swapping SQLite for PostgreSQL later requires only a connection‑string change.
- **Robustness**: Implement retries, timeouts, and structured logging to survive the unpredictable web.
- **Real‑world utility**: The same crawler can power price trackers, academic indexes, or sitemap generators—making it a versatile portfolio piece.

modules.title: Creating a Password Manager with Encryption
modules.content:
## A Breach You Could Have Prevented  

You walk into a coffee shop, pull out your laptop, and open a spreadsheet that contains every login you’ve ever created—plain‑text passwords, email addresses, and security‑question answers. A barista glances over, spots the file, and you both know exactly what could happen next.  

If you had a **password manager** that stored those credentials **encrypted** with a master password derived from a strong key‑stretching algorithm, the data would be useless to anyone without that one secret. Building such a tool yourself not only eliminates the human‑error risk of reusing passwords, it also gives you full control over the cryptographic choices and the data lifecycle.

Below we’ll walk through a complete, production‑ready password manager written in Python 3.10+. The design leans on the tooling and best‑practice foundations you’ve already set up in earlier chapters (Poetry for dependency management, Black & isort for formatting, type hints for static analysis, etc.), and it adds a **secure CLI**, **strong password generation**, **strength checking**, **encrypted SQLite storage**, and optional **sharing** and **recovery** features.

---

## 1. Threat Model & Design Goals  

| Threat | Mitigation |
|--------|------------|
| **Database theft** – attacker gains raw file | Encrypt the entire payload with **AES‑256‑GCM**; store only the ciphertext and a nonce. |
| **Master‑password brute‑force** | Derive the encryption key with a memory‑hard KDF (**Argon2id**) or a proven PBKDF2 implementation with high iteration count. |
| **In‑memory snooping** | Zero out sensitive variables after use (`del`, `ctypes.memset`). |
| **Credential sharing abuse** | Encrypt shared entries with a **public‑key** (RSA‑OAEP) so only the intended recipient can decrypt. |
| **Loss of master password** | Offer a **recovery token** generated from a secret‑sharing scheme (Shamir) that can reconstruct the master key. |

The manager will therefore:

1. Prompt for a master password each session.
2. Derive a symmetric key using **Argon2id** (fallback to PBKDF2 if Argon2 not available).
3. Store credentials in an **SQLite** database, with each row encrypted individually.
4. Provide a **Typer‑based CLI** for CRUD operations, password generation, and strength feedback.
5. Include optional **sharing** and **recovery** commands.

---

## 2. Project Skeleton  

Leverage the **Poetry** template you adopted in *Setting Up a Professional Python Development Environment*:

```bash
poetry new password-manager --src
cd password-manager
poetry add cryptography[hazmat] argon2-cffi typer sqlalchemy
poetry add --dev pytest black flake8 mypy
```

Directory layout (trimmed for brevity):

```
password_manager/
├─ src/
│  ├─ password_manager/
│  │  ├─ __init__.py
│  │  ├─ cli.py          # Typer entry point
│  │  ├─ crypto.py       # KDF, encryption, decryption
│  │  ├─ models.py       # SQLAlchemy ORM
│  │  ├─ storage.py      # DB helpers
│  │  └─ utils.py        # generation, strength checking
│  └─ __main__.py        # `python -m password_manager`
├─ tests/
│  └─ …
├─ pyproject.toml
└─ README.md
```

All modules are **type‑annotated** and formatted with **Black**; static analysis with **mypy** ensures the cryptographic API is used correctly.

---

## 3. Cryptographic Core  

### 3.1 Key Derivation  

```python
# src/password_manager/crypto.py
import os
from typing import Tuple
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.kdf.argon2 import Argon2id
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.kdf.pbkdf2 import PBKDF2HMAC
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives import hashes

SALT_SIZE = 16
KEY_SIZE = 32  # AES‑256

def _load_salt(path: str) -> bytes:
    if os.path.exists(path):
        return open(path, "rb").read()
    salt = os.urandom(SALT_SIZE)
    open(path, "wb").write(salt)
    return salt

def derive_key(master_pw: str, salt_path: str = "salt.bin") -> bytes:
    """Derive a 256‑bit key from the master password."""
    salt = _load_salt(salt_path)
    password_bytes = master_pw.encode()
    try:
        # Prefer Argon2id (memory‑hard, resistant to GPU attacks)
        kdf = Argon2id(
            time_cost=2,
            memory_cost=102400,  # 100 MiB
            parallelism=8,
            length=KEY_SIZE,
            salt=salt,
        )
    except Exception:  # Argon2 not available
        kdf = PBKDF2HMAC(
            algorithm=hashes.SHA256(),
            length=KEY_SIZE,
            salt=salt,
            iterations=200_000,
        )
    return kdf.derive(password_bytes)
```

*Why Argon2id?* It deliberately consumes both CPU and RAM, making large‑scale brute‑force attempts expensive. The fallback to PBKDF2 with 200 k iterations still offers substantial work factor for most attackers.

### 3.2 Symmetric Encryption  

```python
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers.aead import AESGCM

def encrypt(plaintext: bytes, key: bytes) -> Tuple[bytes, bytes]:
    """Return (nonce, ciphertext)."""
    nonce = os.urandom(12)            # Recommended size for GCM
    aesgcm = AESGCM(key)
    ciphertext = aesgcm.encrypt(nonce, plaintext, None)
    return nonce, ciphertext

def decrypt(nonce: bytes, ciphertext: bytes, key: bytes) -> bytes:
    aesgcm = AESGCM(key)
    return aesgcm.decrypt(nonce, ciphertext, None)
```

AES‑GCM provides **confidentiality** and **integrity** in a single primitive, eliminating the need for separate MAC handling.

---

## 4. Data Model & Encrypted Persistence  

### 4.1 SQLAlchemy Schema  

```python
# src/password_manager/models.py
from sqlalchemy import Column, Integer, LargeBinary, String, create_engine
from sqlalchemy.orm import declarative_base, sessionmaker

Base = declarative_base()

class Credential(Base):
    __tablename__ = "credentials"
    id = Column(Integer, primary_key=True)
    site = Column(String, nullable=False)
    username = Column(String, nullable=False)
    nonce = Column(LargeBinary, nullable=False)          # 12‑byte GCM nonce
    ciphertext = Column(LargeBinary, nullable=False)    # Encrypted payload

engine = create_engine("sqlite:///vault.db", future=True, echo=False)
Session = sessionmaker(bind=engine, future=True)

def init_db() -> None:
    Base.metadata.create_all(engine)
```

Only the **nonce** and **ciphertext** are persisted; the plaintext never touches the disk.

### 4.2 Storing & Retrieving Credentials  

```python
# src/password_manager/storage.py
import json
from .crypto import encrypt, decrypt
from .models import Credential, Session, init_db
from typing import List, Tuple

def add_credential(site: str, username: str, password: str, key: bytes) -> None:
    payload = json.dumps({"username": username, "password": password}).encode()
    nonce, ct = encrypt(payload, key)
    cred = Credential(site=site, username=username, nonce=nonce, ciphertext=ct)
    with Session() as s:
        s.add(cred)
        s.commit()

def get_credential(site: str, key: bytes) -> Tuple[str, str]:
    with Session() as s:
        cred = s.query(Credential).filter_by(site=site).first()
        if not cred:
            raise KeyError(f"No entry for {site}")
        plaintext = decrypt(cred.nonce, cred.ciphertext, key)
        data = json.loads(plaintext)
        return data["username"], data["password"]
```

All database interaction is wrapped in a context manager, mirroring the pattern used in earlier chapters (e.g., the RESTful API’s session handling).

---

## 5. CLI Interface with Typer  

The CLI mirrors the **Click/Typer** patterns introduced in *Building a Command Line Tool*.

```python
# src/password_manager/cli.py
import typer
from .utils import generate_password, check_strength
from .storage import add_credential, get_credential, init_db
from .crypto import derive_key

app = typer.Typer(add_completion=False)

def _load_key(master_pw: str) -> bytes:
    return derive_key(master_pw)

@app.command()
def init(master: str = typer.Option(..., prompt=True, hide_input=True)):
    """Create the salt file and initialise the DB."""
    init_db()
    derive_key(master)  # generates salt if missing
    typer.echo("Vault initialized.")

@app.command()
def add(
    site: str,
    username: str,
    password: str = typer.Option(None, prompt=True, hide_input=True),
    master: str = typer.Option(..., prompt=True, hide_input=True),
):
    """Store a new credential."""
    key = _load_key(master)
    add_credential(site, username, password, key)
    typer.echo(f"Credential for {site} added.")

@app.command()
def get(site: str, master: str = typer.Option(..., prompt=True, hide_input=True)):
    """Retrieve a credential."""
    key = _load_key(master)
    user, pw = get_credential(site, key)
    typer.echo(f"Site: {site}\nUser: {user}\nPassword: {pw}")

@app.command()
def gen(
    length: int = typer.Option(16, "--length", "-l", help="Password length"),
    symbols: bool = typer.Option(True, "--symbols/--no-symbols"),
):
    """Generate a strong password."""
    pw = generate_password(length, symbols)
    typer.echo(pw)

@app.command()
def strength(pw: str = typer.Argument(...)):
    """Show a quick strength rating."""
    rating = check_strength(pw)
    typer.echo(f"Strength: {rating}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    app()
```

Running `python -m password_manager` launches the CLI. The `init` command ensures the salt file exists before any credentials are added. All master‑password prompts are hidden, preventing shoulder‑surfing.

---

## 6. Password Generation & Strength Checking  

### 6.1 Generation  

```python
# src/password_manager/utils.py
import secrets
import string

def generate_password(length: int = 16, symbols: bool = True) -> str:
    alphabet = string.ascii_letters + string.digits
    if symbols:
        alphabet += string.punctuation
    return "".join(secrets.choice(alphabet) for _ in range(length))
```

`secrets.choice` draws from a cryptographically secure RNG, unlike `random.choice`.

### 6.2 Strength Estimation  

Instead of pulling in a heavy external library, we implement a lightweight estimator based on **entropy** and **common‑pattern detection**:

```python
import re
import math

COMMON_PATTERNS = [
    r"\d{4,}",               # long runs of digits
    r"(?:[a-z]{3,})",       # dictionary words (simplified)
    r"[!@#$%^&*]{2,}",      # repeated symbols
]

def entropy(pw: str) -> float:
    pool = 0
    if any(c.islower() for c in pw): pool += 26
    if any(c.isupper() for c in pw): pool += 26
    if any(c.isdigit() for c in pw): pool += 10
    if any(c in string.punctuation for c in pw): pool += len(string.punctuation)
    return math.log2(pool) * len(pw)

def check_strength(pw: str) -> str:
    e = entropy(pw)
    for pat in COMMON_PATTERNS:
        if re.search(pat, pw):
            return "Weak (pattern detected)"
    if e < 50:
        return "Weak"
    elif e < 80:
        return "Moderate"
    else:
        return "Strong"
```

The estimator offers immediate feedback in the `strength` command and can be reused by the `add` command to warn users before storing a low‑entropy password.

---

## 7. Advanced Features  

### 7.1 Secure Sharing  

Sharing a credential with another user involves **public‑key encryption**. We use RSA‑OAEP for its simplicity and wide support.

```python
# src/password_manager/sharing.py
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric import rsa, padding
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives import serialization, hashes

def generate_rsa_keypair() -> Tuple[bytes, bytes]:
    private = rsa.generate_private_key(public_exponent=65537, key_size=2048)
    pub = private.public_key()
    priv_pem = private.private_bytes(
        encoding=serialization.Encoding.PEM,
        format=serialization.PrivateFormat.PKCS8,
        encryption_algorithm=serialization.NoEncryption(),
    )
    pub_pem = pub.public_bytes(
        encoding=serialization.Encoding.PEM,
        format=serialization.PublicFormat.SubjectPublicKeyInfo,
    )
    return priv_pem, pub_pem

def encrypt_for_peer(plaintext: bytes, peer_pub_pem: bytes) -> bytes:
    pub_key = serialization.load_pem_public_key(peer_pub_pem)
    return pub_key.encrypt(
        plaintext,
        padding.OAEP(mgf=padding.MGF1(algorithm=hashes.SHA256()), algorithm=hashes.SHA256(), label=None),
    )

def decrypt_from_peer(ciphertext: bytes, own_priv_pem: bytes) -> bytes:
    priv_key = serialization.load_pem_private_key(own_priv_pem, password=None)
    return priv_key.decrypt(
        ciphertext,
        padding.OAEP(mgf=padding.MGF1(algorithm=hashes.SHA256()), algorithm=hashes.SHA256(), label=None),
    )
```

A new CLI command `share` can:

1. Export the receiver’s public key (`share export-key`).
2. Encrypt the selected credential’s plaintext with that key.
3. Output a base64‑encoded blob that the receiver can import via `share import`.

Because the **shared blob** never contains the master password or the AES key, the sender’s vault remains fully protected.

### 7.2 Recovery Token (Shamir Secret Sharing)  

To guard against master‑password loss, we generate a **recovery token** split into three shares, any two of which can reconstruct the key.

```python
# src/password_manager/recovery.py
from secretsharing import SecretSharer

def create_recovery_token(key: bytes, shares: int = 3, threshold: int = 2) -> List[str]:
    hex_key = key.hex()
    return SecretSharer.split_secret(hex_key, threshold, shares)

def recover_key(shares: List[str]) -> bytes:
    hex_key = SecretSharer.recover_secret(shares)
    return bytes.fromhex(hex_key)
```

The `init` command can optionally print the three shares (or write them to separate files). Later, a `recover` command asks for any two shares, reconstructs the key, and re‑derives the master password for the session.

> **Note:** The `secretsharing` package is a pure‑Python implementation; for production environments you might replace it with a vetted C‑extension or hardware‑backed secret store.

---

## 8. Putting It All Together – A Real‑World Walkthrough  

### Scenario: Onboarding a New Team Member  

1. **Initialize the vault** (once per team):  
   ```bash
   $ python -m password_manager init
   Master password: ********
   Vault initialized.
   ```
2. **Add a credential** for the internal Git server:  
   ```bash
   $ python -m password_manager add git.example.com \
       --username alice \
       --master ********
   Password: ********
   Credential for git.example.com added.
   ```
3. **Generate a secure password** for a new service:  
   ```bash
   $ python -m password_manager gen -l 24
   V$9k&bP2q!Zs7*LmX0a#tR4y
   ```
   The output is immediately copied into the service’s signup page.

4. **Share the Git credential** with Bob:  
   ```bash
   $ python -m password_manager share export-key bob_pub.pem
   $ python -m password_manager share git.example.com \
       --peer-key bob_pub.pem \
       --master ******** > git_cred_for_bob.b64
   ```
   Bob runs `share import` with his private key, and the credential is added to his local vault without ever exposing the master password.

5. **Recover after a lost master password** (using two shares):  
   ```bash
   $ python -m password_manager recover
   Share 1: 5f3c9e...
   Share 2: a94b2d...
   Master password recovered. You may now reset it.
   ```

Through these steps the manager demonstrates **end‑to‑end encryption**, **secure sharing**, and **robust recovery**—all from the command line.

---

## 9. Testing & Hardening  

* **Unit tests** (pytest) should cover:  
  - KDF output consistency.  
  - Encryption/decryption round‑trip.  
  - Database CRUD operations.  
  - Sharing encryption/decryption.  
  - Recovery reconstruction.

* **Static analysis**: Run `mypy src/password_manager` and `flake8` to enforce type safety and PEP 8 compliance.

* **Security audit checklist**:  
  - Verify that the salt file is **chmod 600** (owner‑only).  
  - Ensure the SQLite file is also `chmod 600`.  
  - Confirm that the master password is never logged (Typer respects hidden inputs).  
  - Periodically rotate the Argon2 parameters as hardware improves.

* **Continuous Integration**: Add a GitHub Actions workflow that runs the test suite, linter, and type checker on every push—mirroring the CI setup you used for the FastAPI project.

---

## 10. Deployment Considerations  

Even though this tool is CLI‑only, you may want to distribute it as a **stand‑alone binary** for non‑technical users. Tools like **PyInstaller** or **briefcase** can bundle the interpreter and dependencies into a single executable. When packaging:

- **Exclude** the development dependencies (`pytest`, `black`).  
- Sign the binary with a code‑signing certificate to avoid tampering warnings.  
- Provide a **README** that explains the importance of backing up the recovery shares and the salt file.

If you later decide to expose the vault via an API (e.g., for mobile clients), you can reuse the same `crypto.py` and `models.py` modules inside a FastAPI service—showcasing the reusability of the cryptographic core across projects.

---

## Key Takeaways  

- **Derive encryption keys** from a master password with a memory‑hard KDF (Argon2id preferred; PBKDF2 as fallback).  
- **Encrypt each credential** using AES‑256‑GCM; store only nonce + ciphertext in SQLite.  
- **Typer** provides a clean, typed CLI that integrates master‑password prompting, password generation, and strength feedback.  
- **Secure sharing** is achieved with RSA‑OAEP, while **recovery** can be implemented via Shamir secret sharing.  
- Leverage the **Poetry** workflow, Black formatting, and mypy type checking you already set up for a production‑grade codebase.  

By following this chapter, you now have a fully functional, cryptographically sound password manager that can serve as a solid portfolio piece and a foundation for future, more complex security projects.

modules.title: Building a Real-time Data Processing System
modules.content:
## The Real‑World Hook: Detecting Anomalous Transactions as They Happen  

Imagine a fintech startup that must flag potentially fraudulent credit‑card transactions **within seconds** of their arrival. A delayed batch job is not an option; the business needs a pipeline that ingests each event, enriches it, runs a sliding‑window risk score, and pushes the result to a live dashboard for analysts. Building such a pipeline from scratch is a perfect way to showcase a real‑time data processing system and, more importantly, to add a compelling project to your portfolio.

The remainder of this chapter walks you through exactly that pipeline—using either **Apache Kafka** or **RabbitMQ** as the transport layer, processing streams with pure Python, performing windowed aggregations, visualising the flow live, and preparing the whole stack for cloud deployment.

---

## 1. Choosing and Bootstrapping the Message Broker  

Both Kafka and RabbitMQ are battle‑tested, but they differ in semantics:

| Feature | Kafka | RabbitMQ |
|---------|-------|----------|
| **Model** | Append‑only log, partitioned topics | Queue‑based, exchanges & routing keys |
| **Ordering** | Guarantees per‑partition order | No built‑in ordering (can be enforced with single consumer) |
| **Retention** | Time‑ or size‑based retention, replay possible | Messages removed once acknowledged |
| **Throughput** | Very high (hundreds of k msgs/s) | Good for moderate loads, easier to set up for small projects |

For a portfolio project, **Docker Compose** gives you a one‑click environment for either broker. Below is a minimal `docker-compose.yml` that spins up both options; you’ll comment out the service you don’t need.

```yaml
version: "3.9"
services:
  kafka:
    image: confluentinc/cp-kafka:7.5.0
    environment:
      KAFKA_BROKER_ID: 1
      KAFKA_ZOOKEEPER_CONNECT: zookeeper:2181
      KAFKA_ADVERTISED_LISTENERS: PLAINTEXT://kafka:9092
    ports:
      - "9092:9092"
    depends_on:
      - zookeeper

  zookeeper:
    image: confluentinc/cp-zookeeper:7.5.0
    environment:
      ZOOKEEPER_CLIENT_PORT: 2181
    ports:
      - "2181:2181"

  rabbitmq:
    image: rabbitmq:3-management
    ports:
      - "5672:5672"   # AMQP
      - "15672:15672" # Management UI
```

> **Tip:** The project’s `pyproject.toml` (see the *Why Poetry?* chapter) already includes `docker` as a dev dependency, so you can run `poetry run docker compose up -d` from the repository root.

### 1.1 Creating Topics / Queues  

```bash
# Kafka: create a topic named "transactions"
docker exec -it $(docker ps -qf "name=kafka") \
  kafka-topics --create --topic transactions --bootstrap-server kafka:9092 --partitions 3 --replication-factor 1

# RabbitMQ: declare a durable queue "transactions" via the management UI or CLI
docker exec -it $(docker ps -qf "name=rabbitmq") \
  rabbitmqadmin declare queue name=transactions durable=true
```

Both commands are idempotent; running them repeatedly won’t cause errors.

---

## 2. Producing a Stream of Sample Data  

A realistic data generator helps you test the whole pipeline. The following script uses **`confluent-kafka`** for Kafka and **`pika`** for RabbitMQ. It emits JSON‑encoded transaction records every 200 ms.

```python
# src/producer.py
import json, random, time, uuid
from datetime import datetime
from pathlib import Path

# Choose the backend via an env var (default to kafka)
import os
USE_KAFKA = os.getenv("USE_KAFKA", "true").lower() == "true"

if USE_KAFKA:
    from confluent_kafka import Producer
    producer = Producer({"bootstrap.servers": "localhost:9092"})
    def send(msg):
        producer.produce("transactions", msg.encode())
        producer.flush()
else:
    import pika
    connection = pika.BlockingConnection(pika.ConnectionParameters("localhost"))
    channel = connection.channel()
    channel.queue_declare(queue="transactions", durable=True)
    def send(msg):
        channel.basic_publish(
            exchange="",
            routing_key="transactions",
            body=msg.encode(),
            properties=pika.BasicProperties(delivery_mode=2),
        )

def random_transaction():
    return {
        "id": str(uuid.uuid4()),
        "timestamp": datetime.utcnow().isoformat(),
        "amount": round(random.uniform(5, 5000), 2),
        "currency": random.choice(["USD", "EUR", "GBP"]),
        "merchant": random.choice(["Amazon", "Walmart", "Target", "BestBuy"]),
        "card_country": random.choice(["US", "DE", "GB", "FR"]),
        "is_fraud": random.random() < 0.02,  # 2 % synthetic fraud rate
    }

if __name__ == "__main__":
    while True:
        txn = random_transaction()
        send(json.dumps(txn))
        time.sleep(0.2)
```

Run it with `poetry run python -m src.producer`. The script demonstrates **production‑ready patterns** you already saw in the *FastAPI* chapter—environment‑driven configuration, graceful shutdown (add a signal handler), and JSON serialization.

---

## 3. Consuming and Processing the Stream  

Processing can be done with several libraries, but for a pure‑Python approach that still offers **windowed semantics**, **Faust** (Kafka Streams) is ideal. For RabbitMQ, we’ll build a lightweight async consumer using **`aio-pika`** and manually manage windows.

### 3.1 Faust‑Based Processor (Kafka)

```python
# src/processor_faust.py
import faust
import json
from datetime import datetime, timedelta

app = faust.App(
    "fraud-detector",
    broker="kafka://localhost:9092",
    value_serializer="raw",   # we’ll decode manually
)

class Transaction(faust.Record):
    id: str
    timestamp: str
    amount: float
    currency: str
    merchant: str
    card_country: str
    is_fraud: bool

transactions = app.topic("transactions", value_type=Transaction)

# Tumbling window of 1 minute, aggregating total amount per merchant
windowed_totals = (
    transactions
    .group_by(Transaction.merchant)
    .windowed_tumbling(timedelta(minutes=1))
    .aggregate(lambda: 0.0, lambda agg, txn: agg + txn.amount)
)

# Sliding window of 30 seconds, step 10 seconds → risk score
risk_scores = (
    transactions
    .group_by(lambda txn: txn.card_country)
    .windowed_sliding(timedelta(seconds=30), timedelta(seconds=10))
    .aggregate(
        lambda: {"count": 0, "fraud": 0},
        lambda agg, txn: {
            "count": agg["count"] + 1,
            "fraud": agg["fraud"] + int(txn.is_fraud),
        },
    )
)

@app.agent(transactions)
async def detect_fraud(stream):
    async for txn in stream:
        # Simple rule: flag if amount > $3000 or fraud ratio > 30 % in last window
        if txn.amount > 3000:
            print(f"[ALERT] Large transaction {txn.id} – ${txn.amount}")
        # risk score lookup (example only)
        window = risk_scores[txn.card_country].now()
        if window and window["count"] > 0:
            fraud_ratio = window["fraud"] / window["count"]
            if fraud_ratio > 0.3:
                print(f"[ALERT] High fraud ratio for {txn.card_country}: {fraud_ratio:.0%}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.main()
```

Run the app with `poetry run python -m src.processor_faust`. Faust automatically handles **stateful windows**, checkpointing, and graceful restarts—concepts you touched on when building the *Task Scheduler* with Celery.

### 3.2 Async Consumer with Manual Windows (RabbitMQ)

```python
# src/processor_rabbit.py
import asyncio, json, os
from collections import defaultdict, deque
from datetime import datetime, timedelta

import aio_pika

WINDOW_SIZE = timedelta(seconds=30)
STEP = timedelta(seconds=10)

# In‑memory structure: {key: deque[(timestamp, value)]}
windows = defaultdict(deque)

async def process_message(message: aio_pika.IncomingMessage):
    async with message.process():
        txn = json.loads(message.body)
        ts = datetime.fromisoformat(txn["timestamp"])
        key = txn["card_country"]
        windows[key].append((ts, txn["is_fraud"]))

        # Trim old entries
        cutoff = datetime.utcnow() - WINDOW_SIZE
        while windows[key] and windows[key][0][0] < cutoff:
            windows[key].popleft()

        # Compute sliding aggregates every STEP seconds
        now = datetime.utcnow()
        if now.second % STEP.seconds == 0:
            frauds = sum(v for _, v in windows[key])
            total = len(windows[key])
            ratio = frauds / total if total else 0
            if ratio > 0.3:
                print(f"[ALERT] {key} high fraud ratio: {ratio:.0%}")

async def main():
    connection = await aio_pika.connect_robust(
        os.getenv("RABBIT_URL", "amqp://guest:guest@localhost/")
    )
    channel = await connection.channel()
    queue = await channel.declare_queue("transactions", durable=True)

    async with queue.iterator() as queue_iter:
        async for message in queue_iter:
            await process_message(message)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())
```

The RabbitMQ version illustrates **window management without a dedicated streaming library**, reinforcing how you can implement custom logic when the broker lacks native windowing.

---

## 4. Real‑Time Visualization  

A live dashboard turns raw alerts into actionable insight. You already built a Plotly Dash dashboard (Chapter 6); we’ll extend it to consume a **Server‑Sent Events (SSE)** endpoint exposed by a tiny FastAPI service that forwards aggregation results.

### 4.1 FastAPI SSE Endpoint  

```python
# src/api/stream.py
from fastapi import APIRouter, Request
from fastapi.responses import EventSourceResponse
import asyncio

router = APIRouter()

# Shared asyncio.Queue where processors push summary dicts
summary_queue: asyncio.Queue[dict] = asyncio.Queue(maxsize=100)

@router.get("/events")
async def events(request: Request):
    async def event_generator():
        while True:
            # If client disconnects, break the loop
            if await request.is_disconnected():
                break
            try:
                summary = await asyncio.wait_for(summary_queue.get(), timeout=5.0)
                yield f"data: {summary}\n\n"
            except asyncio.TimeoutError:
                # Keep‑alive comment to avoid proxy timeouts
                yield ": keep-alive\n\n"
    return EventSourceResponse(event_generator())
```

In the Faust processor, after computing a windowed aggregate, push it onto `summary_queue`:

```python
# Inside detect_fraud agent, after computing fraud_ratio:
await summary_queue.put(
    {
        "country": txn.card_country,
        "ratio": fraud_ratio,
        "timestamp": datetime.utcnow().isoformat(),
    }
)
```

### 4.2 Dash Front‑End  

```python
# src/dashboard/app.py
import dash
from dash import dcc, html
import dash_bootstrap_components as dbc
import json
import requests

app = dash.Dash(__name__, external_stylesheets=[dbc.themes.BOOTSTRAP])

app.layout = dbc.Container(
    [
        html.H2("Live Fraud Ratio per Country"),
        dcc.Graph(id="live-graph", figure={"data": [], "layout": {"title": "Fraud Ratio"}}),
        dcc.Interval(id="interval", interval=2_000, n_intervals=0),
    ]
)

# Simple client that reads SSE and stores latest ratios
latest = {}

def fetch_sse():
    import sseclient
    resp = requests.get("http://localhost:8000/events", stream=True)
    client = sseclient.SSEClient(resp)
    for event in client.events():
        data = json.loads(event.data)
        latest[data["country"]] = data["ratio"]
        break  # fetch just one update per call

@app.callback(
    dash.dependencies.Output("live-graph", "figure"),
    dash.dependencies.Input("interval", "n_intervals"),
)
def update_graph(_):
    fetch_sse()
    return {
        "data": [
            {"x": list(latest.keys()), "y": list(latest.values()), "type": "bar", "name": "Fraud Ratio"}
        ],
        "layout": {"title": "Fraud Ratio (last 30 s)"},
    }

if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run_server(debug=True)
```

Running the FastAPI server (`poetry run uvicorn src.api.main:app --reload`) and the dashboard (`poetry run python -m src.dashboard.app`) yields a **real‑time bar chart** that updates every two seconds, reflecting the latest sliding‑window risk scores.

---

## 5. Preparing the System for Cloud Deployment  

While the actual cloud‑deployment chapter comes later, the following checklist ensures that the code you’ve written today will slot into a CI/CD pipeline with minimal friction.

| Component | Cloud‑Ready Adjustments |
|-----------|--------------------------|
| **Broker** | Replace local Docker services with managed offerings (e.g., Confluent Cloud, Amazon MSK, or RabbitMQ on AWS MQ). Store connection strings in environment variables (`KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS`, `RABBIT_URL`). |
| **Producer / Consumer** | Use the same env‑var pattern you employed in the *FastAPI* chapter. Add graceful shutdown hooks (`signal.SIGTERM`) so containers stop cleanly. |
| **Stateful Windows** | Faust stores state in RocksDB on the local filesystem. For cloud, mount a persistent volume or switch to a remote changelog topic (Kafka’s default). |
| **Dashboard** | Deploy the Dash app behind a reverse proxy (NGINX) and expose the FastAPI SSE endpoint on the same domain to avoid CORS issues. |
| **Infrastructure as Code** | Add a `docker-compose.yml` for local dev and a matching `docker-compose.prod.yml` (or Helm chart) that points to cloud‑hosted brokers. |
| **Observability** | Export metrics via **Prometheus** client (`faust.App.metrics`) and add a health endpoint (`/health`) to the FastAPI service—mirroring the pattern used in the *Task Scheduler* chapter. |

All of these steps fit naturally into the **Poetry** workflow you’ve been using: `poetry export -f requirements.txt > requirements.txt` for the Docker image, `poetry run black .` for code style consistency, and `pre-commit` hooks for linting before each push.

---

## 6. Testing the End‑to‑End Pipeline  

A robust test suite gives prospective employers confidence that the system works under load.

1. **Unit Tests** – mock the broker client (`unittest.mock.AsyncMock`) and verify that the processor pushes the correct alert structure onto the queue.
2. **Integration Test** – spin up a temporary Docker Compose stack (`docker compose -f docker-compose.yml up -d`) and run a short‑lived producer that emits 100 records. Assert that the SSE endpoint receives at least one fraud alert.
3. **Load Test** – use **Locust** or **k6** to simulate 5 k messages per second and monitor CPU/memory usage. Adjust the number of Faust partitions accordingly.

Because the repository already includes a `tests/` folder and a `pytest` configuration, you can add a new file `tests/test_processor.py` and run `poetry run pytest`.

---

## 7. Extending the System  

Now that you have a functional pipeline, consider adding any of the following enhancements:

- **Enrichment** – query a Redis cache (or the password manager you built earlier) for user risk profiles before scoring.
- **Machine‑Learning Scoring** – replace the simple rule‑based alert with a scikit‑learn model (Chapter 8) that runs inside the Faust agent.
- **Fault Tolerance** – configure Kafka’s **exactly‑once semantics** (`enable.idempotence=true`) and RabbitMQ’s **dead‑letter exchanges** for failed messages.
- **Multi‑tenant Support** – extend the FastAPI router to accept a `tenant_id` query param and route each tenant’s stream to a dedicated topic/queue.

These ideas illustrate how the real‑time pipeline can evolve into a production‑grade analytics platform.

---

## Key Takeaways  

- **Kafka vs RabbitMQ** – choose based on ordering guarantees and retention needs; both can be launched instantly with Docker Compose.  
- **Producer** – a small Python script using `confluent-kafka` or `pika` can simulate realistic event streams.  
- **Processor** – Faust provides built‑in windowed aggregations for Kafka; with RabbitMQ you can craft async consumers and manage windows manually.  
- **Window Types** – tumbling windows give discrete snapshots; sliding windows enable overlapping risk scores, essential for fraud detection.  
- **Live Dashboard** – FastAPI’s SSE endpoint combined with a Plotly Dash front‑end creates a responsive visual monitoring tool.  
- **Cloud‑Ready Practices** – externalize broker URLs, use environment‑driven configuration, containerize each component, and expose health/metrics endpoints.  
- **Testing** – unit‑mock brokers, run integration tests against a temporary Docker stack, and perform load testing to validate scalability.  

By completing the steps in this chapter you’ll have a **full‑stack, real‑time data processing system** that can be showcased on GitHub, discussed in interviews, and readily extended into a production deployment. Happy streaming!

modules.title: Deploying Python Applications to Cloud Platforms
modules.content:
## From Local Prototype to Global Service  

You’ve just finished the FastAPI‑based news aggregator that scrapes headlines with the multi‑threaded crawler from **Chapter 11**, stores results in PostgreSQL, and offers a clean JSON API. Locally it runs with `poetry run uvicorn app.main:app`.  
Now a client asks: *“Can you make this run 24/7, handle spikes, and give us logs in real time?”*  

The answer lies in three tightly coupled steps:

1. **Package the code in a reproducible container**  
2. **Push the container to a cloud service that can scale**  
3. **Wire the whole thing into an automated CI/CD pipeline with monitoring**  

The sections below walk you through each step, using the same codebase you built earlier. By the end you’ll be able to ship any of the projects from previous chapters—FastAPI APIs, password‑manager back‑ends, or real‑time processing pipelines—into production with a single command.

---

## 1. Containerizing Python Applications with Docker  

### 1.1 Why Docker Matters for Python  

* **Isolation:** No more “works on my machine” surprises—every dependency lives inside the image.  
* **Portability:** The same image runs on your laptop, an EC2 instance, or a Cloud Run service.  
* **Speed:** Layers are cached, so rebuilds after a small code change are near‑instant.  

### 1.2 Building a Minimal, Multi‑Stage Dockerfile  

Because you already use **Poetry** for dependency management, the Dockerfile can stay lean:

```dockerfile
# ---- Builder stage ---------------------------------------------------------
FROM python:3.11-slim AS builder
WORKDIR /app

# Install build tools and Poetry
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y build-essential curl && \
    curl -sSL https://install.python-poetry.org | python3 -

# Copy only the files needed for dependency resolution
COPY pyproject.toml poetry.lock ./
RUN poetry config virtualenvs.create false && \
    poetry install --no-dev --no-interaction --no-ansi

# ---- Runtime stage ---------------------------------------------------------
FROM python:3.11-slim
WORKDIR /app

# Runtime dependencies (e.g., PostgreSQL client)
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y libpq5 && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# Copy the installed packages from the builder
COPY --from=builder /usr/local/lib/python3.11/site-packages /usr/local/lib/python3.11/site-packages
COPY --from=builder /usr/local/bin /usr/local/bin

# Copy application code
COPY . .

# Use a non‑root user for security
RUN useradd -m appuser && chown -R appuser:appuser /app
USER appuser

# Entrypoint – uvicorn with gunicorn workers for production
CMD ["gunicorn", "app.main:app", "-k", "uvicorn.workers.UvicornWorker", "--workers", "4", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000"]
```

**Key points**

* **Multi‑stage build** strips out build‑time packages (gcc, curl) from the final image, reducing size from ~600 MB to <150 MB.  
* **Poetry’s `virtualenvs.create false`** installs directly into the global site‑packages, avoiding an extra layer of indirection.  
* **`gunicorn` + `uvicorn`** gives you a robust production server with graceful reloads and configurable worker counts.  

### 1.3 Local Build & Test  

```bash
docker build -t news-aggregator:dev .
docker run -p 8000:8000 news-aggregator:dev
```

Visit `http://localhost:8000/docs`—the same OpenAPI UI you generated in **Chapter 2**—to verify the container works.

## 2. Choosing a Cloud Platform  

### 2.1 Quick Comparison  

| Feature                     | AWS (ECS/Fargate) | GCP (Cloud Run) | Azure (Container Apps) |
|-----------------------------|-------------------|-----------------|------------------------|
| **Pricing model**           | Pay‑per‑vCPU‑second | Pay‑per‑request + CPU‑seconds | Pay‑per‑vCPU‑second |
| **Managed DNS**             | Route 53          | Cloud DNS       | Azure DNS              |
| **Built‑in logging**        | CloudWatch Logs  | Cloud Logging   | Azure Monitor Logs    |
| **Serverless container**    | Fargate (no servers) | Cloud Run (fully serverless) | Container Apps (serverless) |
| **Native CI/CD integration**| CodeBuild + CodePipeline | Cloud Build | Azure DevOps Pipelines |
| **Best for**                | Complex networking, VPC‑level control | Simple HTTP services, quick scaling | Tight integration with Microsoft ecosystem |

All three providers support Docker images stored in a container registry (ECR, Artifact Registry, or ACR). Pick the one that matches your existing cloud footprint; the steps below focus on AWS because it offers the most granular control for multi‑service architectures (e.g., a FastAPI front‑end plus a Celery worker).

### 2.2 Deploying to AWS Fargate (Step‑by‑Step)

1. **Create a repository in Amazon Elastic Container Registry (ECR)**  

   ```bash
   aws ecr create-repository --repository-name news-aggregator
   ```

2. **Tag and push the image**  

   ```bash
   $(aws ecr get-login --no-include-email)   # Authenticate Docker
   docker tag news-aggregator:dev <account-id>.dkr.ecr.<region>.amazonaws.com/news-aggregator:latest
   docker push <account-id>.dkr.ecr.<region>.amazonaws.com/news-aggregator:latest
   ```

3. **Define an ECS task definition** (JSON snippet)

   ```json
   {
     "family": "news-aggregator",
     "networkMode": "awsvpc",
     "requiresCompatibilities": ["FARGATE"],
     "cpu": "512",
     "memory": "1024",
     "containerDefinitions": [
       {
         "name": "api",
         "image": "<account-id>.dkr.ecr.<region>.amazonaws.com/news-aggregator:latest",
         "portMappings": [{ "containerPort": 8000, "protocol": "tcp" }],
         "environment": [
           { "name": "DATABASE_URL", "value": "postgres://user:pass@db-instance:5432/news" },
           { "name": "REDIS_URL", "value": "redis://redis-instance:6379/0" }
         ],
         "logConfiguration": {
           "logDriver": "awslogs",
           "options": {
             "awslogs-group": "/ecs/news-aggregator",
             "awslogs-region": "<region>",
             "awslogs-stream-prefix": "ecs"
           }
         }
       }
     ]
   }
   ```

4. **Create a Fargate service**  

   ```bash
   aws ecs create-service \
     --cluster default \
     --service-name news-aggregator \
     --task-definition news-aggregator \
     --desired-count 2 \
     --launch-type FARGATE \
     --network-configuration "awsvpcConfiguration={subnets=[subnet-abc],securityGroups=[sg-xyz],assignPublicIp=ENABLED}"
   ```

5. **Expose via an Application Load Balancer (ALB)** – map port 80 → container 8000, enable health‑check `/health`.

**One‑click equivalents**  
* **GCP Cloud Run**: `gcloud run deploy news-aggregator --image <image> --platform managed --allow-unauthenticated`.  
* **Azure Container Apps**: `az containerapp create --name news-aggregator --image <image> --environment <env> --ingress external --target-port 8000`.
